text.p: Juventus player profiles for Wednesday's European Cup final against Borussia Dortmund in Munich:

Angelo Perruzzi, goalkeeper, 27. A fundamental element in the Juventus success story, Peruzzi is currently in top form. He is widely considered the best goalkeeper in Italy, an opinion shared by Italian manager Cesare Maldini, for whom he is the number one choice.

Michelangelo Rampulla, reserve goalkeeper, 34. An accomplished reserve now in his fifth season at Juventus, Rampulla has occasionally stepped in for important European Cup ties, most notably when playing well in a 2-1 UEFA Cup semifinal win against Borussia Dortmund in April 1995.

Sergio Porrini, right back, 28. This is Porrini's fourth season of European competition with Juventus and his experience is likely to earn him a place against Dortmund ahead of the much less experienced Mark Iuliano. A versatile player, Porrini can play anywhere in defence, while he is also useful with his head when he moves forward for set-kicks.

Ciro Ferrara, central defender, 30. One of the rocks on which the Juventus success story has been founded. A player who grew up alongside Diego Maradona at Napoli, Ferrara is not only vastly experienced but is also gifted with good positional sense, good timing and immense physical presence. Currently at his best and currently also a key figure in Cesare Maldini's Italy side.

Paolo Montero, central defender, 25. Uruguyan Montero's first season at Juventus, after four seasons with Atalanta, has proved an unqualified success. Tough, resolute and not averse to kicking shins, Montero's defensive partnership with Ferrara is crucial to the Juventus team balance.

Gianluca Pessotto, left back, 26. In his second season with Juventus, Pessotto is coach Marcello Lippi's normal first choice at left back. Only his injury interrupted season casts doubt on his presence against Dortmund, but his experience should see get the nod ahead of Iuliano.

Mark Iuliano, reserve defender, 23. Something of an unknown quantity when bought from second division Salernitana last season, Iuliano has played in 21 Serie A games, with his best moment undoubtedly coming last Friday night when he scored the equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Atalanta that gave Juventus a 24th title. Likely to start on the bench.

Angelo Di Livio, right-side midfield, 30. Known as the "Little Soldier" because of his wholehearted commitment and workrate, Di Livio has been a constant feature in Juventus sides of the last four seasons. Not only vital as defensive cover but capable of getting to the byeline before sending in useful crosses for the head of Christian Vieri.

Didier Deschamps, central midfielder, 28. The motor of the Juventus midfield, Frenchman Deschamps is not just a runner and fetcher but also a highly skilled traffic controller. He has filled the gap left by the departure last summer of Portughese midfielder Paulo Sousa while his experience has made life easy for his midfield compatriot Zinedine Zidane.

Zinedine Zidane, central playmaker, 24. The attacking, creative element in the Juventus midfield, Frenchman Zidane has had an excellent first season in Italian soccer after the inevitable settling-in period. Poised, balanced and capable of playing off either foot, Zidane has done so well that comparisons have recently been made with an illustrious France and Juventus predecessor, Michel Platini.

Vladimir Jugovic, left-side midfield, 27. When it comes to Champions' Cup finals, Yugoslav Jugovic is the most experienced Juventus player of the lot, having already picked up two winner's medals, first with Red Star Belgrade in 1991 and then last year with Juventus. At the top of his form this season, Jugovic seems a certain first choice.
Antonio Conte, reserve midfielder, 27. Out for most of this season with a serious knee injury, Conte's lack of match fitness will almost certainly rule him out, at least initially.

Attilio Lombardo, reserve midfielder, 31. Although he has finally come back to his best form after a leg break in the summer of 1995, Lombardo starts as a reserve likely to be brought on in a wide role, only if things are going badly

Alessio Tacchinardi, utility reserve, 21. Tacchinardi can play in defence or midfield and thus makes an ideal reserve. A player of immense potential, he is nonetheless likely to start on the substitutes' bench.

Christian Vieri, central striker, 23. Vieri is the only Juventus striker certain of his team place against Dortmund and that fact in itself underlines the progress he has made this season, progress further highlighted by his senior international debut when scoring Italy's 1000th international goal in a 3-0 World Cup win against Moldova in Trieste at Easter. Big, strong but skilful, he is akin to an old fashioned centre forward.

Alen Boksic, striker, 27. On his day, Croat Boksic is one of the most dynamic attacking runners in world soccer. A mid-winter injury, however, has taken the shine from his attacking skills and means that he is in contention with Nicola Amoruso and Alessandro Del Piero for the place alongside Vieri.

Alessandro Del Piero, striker, 22. Still under the shadow of an injury-interrupted season that has seen him miss 77 days, Del Piero does not yet seem back to the sort of form which earned him the knickname, Pinturichio, after the renaissance painter. Despite his obvious class and experience, he could start as a substitute.

Nicola Amoruso, striker, 23. Like Vieri, he has made remarkable progress this season and could yet edge his way into the side in front of both Boksic and Del Piero. Scored important goals in both semi-final ties against Dutch side Ajax Amsterdam. If Vieri is the bludgeon, he is the rapier.
